precepts.text: Abram, childless, meant to leave his house to Eliezer of Damascus, the eldest servant born in his house; the Lord said this shall not be thine heir, but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels; an heir and an inheritance are the same word.
precepts.point: It is written there to exclude, not to include; it does not mean the Egyptian became a Jew, and when we came back under the Persians a man who could not show his father's house got no inheritance and no office.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Abram, childless, was going to leave his house to Eliezer of Damascus, the eldest servant born in his house: “Behold, to me thou hast given no seed: and, lo, one born in my house is mine heir.” The Lord said no: “This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir.” Not a heathen servant, but his own seed. An heir and an inheritance are the same word, like a family heirloom passed down the line.

That is the key to 1 Chronicles 2: “Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha. And Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife.” This was while Israel was in Egypt, when we had no land of inheritance allotted to us. People read it and say the Egyptian married into the tribe and became Judah. No.

The record follows that line for generation after generation so that it is known. When Israel came out of Egypt and inherited the land, that line could not receive land, because the land passes by the paternal bloodline and that line goes back to an Egyptian servant. They were among us in the land, but they did not inherit. It is written there to exclude, not to include. Sheshan's brothers had sons and received land; his line did not. It does not mean the Egyptian became a Jew. When we came back under the Persians and the Medes, a man who could not show from his father's house who he came from was given no inheritance, and a Levite could not serve in his office. Zerubbabel could show he came from King David's line.

The daughters of Zelophehad show the law when a man has only daughters. They asked, “Why should the name of our father be done away from among his family, because he hath no son?” The Lord said, “If a man die, and have no son, then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter”, then to his brother, then his father's brethren, then the next kinsman: the law Boaz was fulfilling. But those daughters had to marry “only to the family of the tribe of their father”, “So shall not the inheritance of the children of Israel remove from tribe to tribe.” The inheritance of Israel is paternal. There is no sin in marrying a woman of another tribe; Aaron did it. The command there was only to keep the land in the tribe. We have no land in captivity now, so marry within your nation and stay with your people.

precepts.text: The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair, and took them wives of all which they chose. The wickedness in verse 5 is that mixing the Most High said not to do; it grieved him at his heart, and judgment followed the chosen line into Egypt.
precepts.point: Why did God allow it? Because the sons of God broke God's law before it.

note.label: 70 Times 7: The Perfection of Mercy Through Christ

precepts.why:
Christ spoke to Abram, before his name was changed to Abraham: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years.” That seed runs through Isaac, not through Abraham’s other children; Paul expounds that in Romans 9. The other nations are not God’s chosen people. And this first affliction is not America; it is ancient Egypt, where Jacob and the souls with him walked in.

So why did God bring that judgment on us? What did the sons of God do? They mixed with the daughters of men. Genesis 6: “the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.” The sons of God are the chosen line that came out of Seth, who replaced Abel after Cain killed him.

“There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” Then: “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” The wickedness of verse 5 is that very thing: the sons of God taking the daughters of men to themselves, when the Most High had said not to do it.

“And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” Now we know why the Most High told Abraham that his seed would surely end up serving in Egypt four hundred years. As the sons of God we broke his laws, and he brought forth judgment, rightfully so.

precepts.text: Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God. That is the lineage of the sons of God: the chosen line comes through Seth, who replaced Abel. Write that down so the question never confuses you again.
precepts.point: Why did God allow it? Because the sons of God broke God's law before it.

note.label: 70 Times 7: The Perfection of Mercy Through Christ

precepts.why:
Genesis 6 says “the sons of God saw the daughters of men,” and the question always comes: who are the sons of God, and what line do they come out of? Luke 3:38 answers it at the end of Christ’s genealogy: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.”

That is the lineage of the sons of God. Adam is called the son of God, and the chosen line runs from him through Seth. Of Adam’s sons, Abel was put to death, and Seth replaced him; the sons of God came out of Seth’s line, down to Enos and on to Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Write that down so the next time the question comes up you are not confused. It explains the promise to Abram: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs.” The sons of God of Seth’s line broke God’s law by mixing with the daughters of men, and the judgment came down on the same chosen line: Jacob’s children went into Egypt and served in hard bondage four hundred years.

precepts.text: Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river Euphrates.
precepts.point: Jubilee began only when Israel entered the land, and the land's borders are in the Middle East.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Before Genesis, Deuteronomy 11 was read from verse 21, the word the Lord gave Israel in advance of entering the land: “That your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children, in the land which the Lord sware unto your fathers to give them, as the days of heaven upon the earth.” For us, heaven has always been upon the earth. If Israel would diligently keep the commandments, “Then will the Lord drive out all these nations from before you, and ye shall possess greater nations and mightier than yourselves.” To possess means to own. Then: “Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours”. Every place your feet touch is your land; that is heaven on earth.

With a map on the screen, verse 24 lays out the borders. “From the wilderness” is the wilderness of Egypt, on the other side of the Nile. “And Lebanon” sits at the top of the map, and Lebanon was ours. “from the river, the river Euphrates” runs through Syria, just above Lebanon. “even unto the uttermost sea” is the Mediterranean on the left. So the land ran from the wilderness of Egypt all the way up to the Euphrates, taking in Syria and everything down from it.

Genesis 15:18 goes with Deuteronomy 11:21-24. “In the same day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates”. The river of Egypt is the Nile. The same land God promised Abraham is the land Israel took. We were fighting from the time of Joshua to get all of it, and we fully had it under David and Solomon.

This matters for Jubilee. Jubilee did not start until Israel got into the land: count seven times seven years, forty-nine, and the fiftieth year is the jubilee, when the land rests and every piece of land goes back to the original owner of that heritage, that tribe. So the land has borders, and they are in the Middle East. The doctrines going around that the Congo, or Kenya, is the real Israel cannot stand. What are y'all talking about? It gives you the land layout right here. The hell is this?

From there Isaiah 14 shows the land coming back: “For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land”. He is not having mercy on everybody, only Jacob. We may be at the bottom of society, but he will yet choose Israel, and it is God who sets us in the land, not the League of Nations or the United Nations. “And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place”: every nation goes back to the land God first gave it, and “the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids”. The laws of Leviticus 25 cannot be in effect now while we are the slaves in a foreign land, but when we return to the land they go back into full effect.

precepts.text: Righteousness is immortal; the righteous seed endures forever.
precepts.point: Righteousness is immortal, and righteousness is defined by the law: it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments. Abram's faith showed itself in his works.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
“He believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” And “righteousness is immortal.” The seed Abram was told to count in the stars is a righteous seed, and a righteous seed endures for ever.

Righteousness is not a passing thing. What was counted to Abram when he believed carries on in his seed, as many as the stars of heaven, and it does not die.

precepts.text: It shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments; righteousness goes into keeping the laws.
precepts.point: Righteousness is immortal, and righteousness is defined by the law: it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments. Abram's faith showed itself in his works.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
What is righteousness? The scriptures define it, and it is defined by the law: “it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments before the Lord our God, as he hath commanded us.”

So when Abram believed and “he counted it to him for righteousness”, that righteousness goes into keeping the laws. Abram’s faith was not a feeling; it showed itself in his works, in observing to do what the Lord commanded him.

precepts.text: Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness; his faith was shown in his works.
precepts.point: Righteousness is immortal, and righteousness is defined by the law: it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments. Abram's faith showed itself in his works.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
Paul asks what Abraham our father found “as pertaining to the flesh”, and answers from this very verse: “For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.”

“If Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.” Abraham had no cause to boast in the flesh. He believed the Lord who told him to tell the stars, “So shall thy seed be”, and that belief was counted for righteousness.

And righteousness is defined by the commandments, so his faith was shown in his works. Faith and obedience were never two separate things in Abraham: he believed God, and his belief was seen in what he did.

precepts.text: In a dream, in a vision of the night, He openeth the ears of men and sealeth their instruction.
precepts.point: When the sun went down a deep sleep and a horror of great darkness fell on Abram: he was about to receive a vision of future prophecy. The Most High speaks in a dream, in a vision of the night, and reveals His secret to His servants the prophets.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
Abram had divided the heifer, the goat and the ram, and driven the fowls from the carcases; he was offering sacrifice. Then “when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.” That deep sleep is how the Most High speaks.

Job shows it: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed; Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction.” The deep sleep that fell on Abram was the Most High opening his ears. He was about to receive a vision of future prophecy, the four hundred years of his seed.

precepts.text: The Lord God revealeth His secret unto His servants the prophets.
precepts.point: When the sun went down a deep sleep and a horror of great darkness fell on Abram: he was about to receive a vision of future prophecy. The Most High speaks in a dream, in a vision of the night, and reveals His secret to His servants the prophets.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
“Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.” Abram was His servant, and what came to him in the deep sleep and the horror of great darkness was the Lord revealing His secret: the prophecy of what would befall his seed.

The Lord does nothing without first showing it to His prophets. The sacrifice was laid out, the sun went down, and the Most High revealed to Abram what He was about to do.

precepts.text: His seed should sojourn in a strange land, in bondage, and be evil entreated four hundred years.
precepts.point: Abram himself would go to his fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age; and the seed would return in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
Stephen repeats the prophecy: “God spake on this wise, That his seed should sojourn in a strange land; and that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years.” Same words as Genesis 15:13: a stranger in a land that is not theirs, serving them, afflicted four hundred years.

This was fulfilled in Egypt. Abram was told to “know of a surety” that it would happen to his seed, and Stephen, looking back, shows it did.

precepts.text: The sojourning of the children of Israel in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years, and it ended the selfsame day; the prophecy was fulfilled at the Exodus.
precepts.point: Abram himself would go to his fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age; and the seed would return in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
“The sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.” The four hundred years spoken to Abram was an approximation of that time. “At the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.”

That is the fulfilment of Genesis 15:13. The strange land was Egypt, the affliction was Egypt’s bondage, and it ended at the Exodus, the selfsame day the four hundred and thirty years were up.

So this verse is not the doctrine about America and 1619. The prophecy of the four hundred years was fulfilled when Israel came out of Egypt.

precepts.text: Israel is yet this day in captivity, scattered for a reproach; the scattering did not end on a four hundred year clock.
precepts.point: Abram himself would go to his fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age; and the seed would return in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
“Behold, we are yet this day in our captivity, where thou hast scattered us, for a reproach and a curse, and to be subject to payments, according to all the iniquities of our fathers, which departed from the Lord our God.”

Israel is still in captivity and still scattered this day. The northern kingdom’s captivity on this side began in 1492, and by that counting the years have passed four hundred and Israel is still not out. The scattering did not end on a four hundred year clock, which shows that Genesis 15:13 is not about America and 1619; that prophecy was fulfilled at the Exodus.

The twelve tribes scattered among the nations today, the people called Blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans, are the seed this covenant history belongs to, yet this day in their captivity for a reproach and subject to payments, according to the iniquities of our fathers.

precepts.text: Egypt urged them out in haste, and the Lord gave the people favour, and they spoiled the Egyptians; they came out with great substance.
precepts.point: Abram himself would go to his fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age; and the seed would return in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
“Afterward shall they come out with great substance.” Here is how it happened. “The Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men.” The children of Israel did according to the word of Moses, “and they borrowed of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment.”

“The Lord gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent unto them such things as they required. And they spoiled the Egyptians.” The nation they served was judged, and they walked out of it with the silver, gold and raiment of Egypt, just as the Lord had told Abram: great substance.

precepts.text: Abraham was counted righteous before circumcision was implemented; faith and obedience came first.
precepts.point: It still has to be done. A covenant is a contract with terms; the covenant was confirmed to Jacob for a law, and circumcision is one of the laws within the covenant.

note.label: Genesis 17: The Covenant Sealed in the Flesh

precepts.why:
Two chapters before circumcision was implemented, “he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised. Faith and obedience came first; circumcision came after, as the seal of the righteousness of the faith he already had.

That is why a brother coming into the truth gets built up in the faith first and then goes through with the process. It does not make circumcision optional: “Every man child among you shall be circumcised.” It just shows the order in which Abraham walked it.

precepts.text: Thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them four hundred years; and afterward shall they come out with great substance.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.

note.label: Exodus 2: The Birth of Moses

precepts.why:
God heard their groaning and “God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.” The bondage itself was part of what God told Abraham: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years”.

And the way out was told him too: “And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.” When Israel cried by reason of the bondage, God remembered that word.

That prophecy is about Egypt. It is not a date of release in this present day.

precepts.text: The fourth generation would come hither again, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full; Sihon fell when it was full.
precepts.point: By this point their iniquity was fulfilled, like Babylon whose sins reached unto heaven, so the Lord loosed Israel to come through the land of the Amorites and slay Sihon their king.

note.label: Deuteronomy 1: The Second Giving of the Law

precepts.why:
When the Lord told Abraham his seed would serve four hundred years, he set the time of their return by the Amorites: “But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.” Israel could not come back into the land until the iniquity of the Amorites was full.

By the time Moses declares this law, it was. Their iniquity was fulfilled, like Babylon whose sins reached unto heaven, so the Lord loosed Israel to come through the land of the Amorites and slay “Sihon the king of the Amorites, which dwelt in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan”. That is why the law is declared “After he had slain Sihon”: the fourth generation had come hither again, and Sihon fell when the iniquity of the Amorites was full.

precepts.text: Thy seed shall serve and be afflicted four hundred years and come hither again in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full; the destruction was prophesied and just.
precepts.point: Genesis 15:13 is not talking about America. Judah has been here longer than four hundred years and the northern kingdom longer than six hundred, so this is not us coming up out of Babylon the great; and Israel was actually in Egypt four hundred and thirty years, free for the first thirty.

note.label: Joshua 11: The Northern Kings Utterly Destroyed

precepts.why:
The Most High is not unjust in what he does. It was already prophesied to Abram: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years; And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.” Then: “But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.”

When Israel came back to establish the land, it was time for those nations to pay for their iniquities from way back when. The iniquity of the Amorites was full, and the destruction was prophesied and just.

Genesis 15:13 is not talking about America. Judah has been here longer than four hundred years and the northern kingdom longer than six hundred, so this is not us coming up out of Babylon the great; and Israel was actually in Egypt four hundred and thirty years, free for the first thirty.

precepts.text: The Most High made a covenant with Abram, "Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates," so the restitution restores the land of Israel to its proper owners.
precepts.point: The restitution is tied to the oath and promise, which is us being saved from our enemies and restored to our kingdom and land, because the promise was made to Abraham our father and passed through the royal seed.

note.label: Acts 3: The Restitution of All Things

precepts.why:
“In the same day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates”.

The land was given by covenant to Abraham's seed, with its borders named. Restitution restores something lost or stolen to its proper owner, and the proper owners of the land of Israel are Abraham's seed. The restitution of all things restores the land of Israel to them.

precepts.text: The Most High told Abraham beforehand that his seed would be a stranger in a land not theirs, serve them, and be afflicted four hundred years, and that he would judge that nation; this is the prophecy Stephen is quoting.
precepts.point: Then he gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and so Abraham begat Isaac and circumcised him the eighth day, and Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat the twelve patriarchs.

note.label: Acts 7: Stephen Rehearses the History and the Stiffnecked Resist the Holy Ghost

precepts.why:
Stephen is quoting the prophecy the Most High gave Abraham. “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years”. That is the strange land, the bondage and the four hundred years of being treated evil that Stephen rehearses.

“And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.” The Most High told Abraham beforehand that he would judge the nation they served, and that afterward they would come out. Stephen says the same: that nation he would judge, and after that they would come forth and serve him in this place. The history Stephen rehearses is the word spoken to Abraham, fulfilled.
